        St. John's point guard Quinn Ellis was ruled eligible Tuesday, one day before the Johnnies lace up against Drexel in the season's first exhibition. Ellis, 23, was one of the top targets in free agency after shining in the EuroLeague last season for Olimpia Milano. The 6-foot-4 guard profiles as a high-feel, steadying hand for a St. John's club that had to replace all five starters, including the irreplaceable Zuby Ejiofor. Ellis averaged 8.2 points, 4.3 rebounds and 4.5 assists with just 1.7 turnovers in 36 games competing in the second-best basketball league in the world. Rick Pitino has lofty expectations for Ellis, lumping him right next to Daniss Jenkins and Kadary Richmond — both All-Big East talents — as one of the most talented point guards he's coached at St. John's. With Ellis in the fold, St. John's is prepared to shift its offensive identity to a perimeter-focused attack. Instead of relying on Ejiofor, Bryce Hopkins and Dillon Mitchell to smash opponents into submission with physical drives and a boatload of offensive rebounds, Ellis gives St. John's a chance to be one of the better pick-and-roll offenses in the Big East, especially since he's paired with a knockdown shooter like Ian Jackson and an elite slasher like top-rated Baylor transfer Tounde Yessoufou.Ellis will be one of the highest-paid point guards in all of college basketball next season, but his eligibility had come into scrutiny after the NCAA introduced stricter eligibility guidelines for international prospects in late May … a month after St. John's had landed Ellis' commitment over a horde of other high-major schools. Make no mistake, Ellis was a full-blown professional basketball player. He signed a multi-year deal with Milano in July of 2025, but he was able to get cleared because he was still within his five-year window of graduating high school and had his transcripts in order. Since he is already 23 years old, Ellis will only have one more year of eligibility. Utah's Noam Yaacov (academics) and LSU's Yam Madar (not within the five-year eligibility clock window) are two high-profile examples of the NCAA axing potential international professionals from playing college basketball this season.While they play different positions, Ellis is in a similar boat as 23-year-old Virginia forward Thijs De Ridder, who played professionally in Belgium but was cleared by the NCAA this time last year because he was still within that five-year eligibility clock window. De Ridder went on to lead Virginia in scoring at 15.6 points per game and help flip UVa into a 30-win club. The bruising 4-man is a popular preseason ACC Player of the Year in 2026-27. 
St. John's is hoping for a similar cannonball into college hoops for Ellis, who should team up with Yessoufou and Jackson to give St. John's one of the Big East's most dynamic backcourts. That trio can go toe-to-toe with UConn's electric duo of Silas Demary Jr. and Braylon Mullins. If Pitino's Hall of Fame coaching can vault this new-look St. John's frontcourt into one of the better rebounding clubs in the Big East, the Johnnies could certainly be in the mix to make the Final Four with this high-ceiling backcourt at center stage of the pitch.
An eligible Ellis is a big deal, but Pitino's outfit is not quite out of the woods yet on the eligibility front. Auburn transfer Keyshawn Hall is still fighting for a fifth year of eligibility in the ongoing 5-for-5 case. He is currently eligible to suit up for the Johnnies thanks to a temporary restraining order, but that legal process is still ongoing. Forward Babacar Sane was ruled ineligible by the NCAA because he signed an Exhibit 10 deal with the Utah Jazz in June of 2024, but he never played in a game. Sane is appealing that ruling and has another court hearing scheduled for Nov. 9.St. John's will play Monmouth in the season-opener on Nov. 2.

title: Rory McIlroy in favor of LIV Golf players returning to DP World Tour and PGA Tour - CBS Sports
description: After years of back-and-forth, McIlroy seems content with allowing those who left to come back
body:
After years of back-and-forth, McIlroy seems content with allowing those who left to come back
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    2:19 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        If Rory McIlroy had a vote to allow former members of LIV Golf back on the PGA Tour and DP World Tour, the six-time major champion would say, "yes." Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, India, ahead of this week's DP World Tour event, McIlroy touched on the evolving golf landscape and player movement between circuits as LIV Golf enters its next chapter."Yes, I would [let former LIV Golf players come back]," McIlroy said. "I think a rising tide lifts all boats, and I think having some of these players back is beneficial for the business of the Tours, absolutely."One of LIV Golf's biggest draws the last few years, Jon Rahm, exited from the league last week. The two-time major champion's lawyer announced during the LIV Golf bankruptcy hearing that his client had no interest moving forward with LIV Golf 2.0 as he found the terms "unacceptable."Rahm is one of a handful of LIV Golf players to have playing privileges on the DP World Tour, along with Tyrrell Hatton, Tom McKibbin and Adrian Meronk. Rahm will be able to play on the DP World Tour in 2027, but the PGA Tour may not be as welcoming, as the league has typically issued one-year suspensions to those who played on LIV Golf."I think the thing that people have to realize is that both the PGA Tour and the DP World Tour are both membership organizations," McIlroy said. "And the leadership of both those organizations need to go to the members and say to them, 'OK, what would you like to see?'
"On one hand, I'm sure some members that stayed loyal would feel hard done by if these guys can just walk straight back in, but then on the other side, having these players back on your tour is very good for business and that can drive revenues up and then everyone can benefit from that. So, there certainly is a balance there."McIlroy's comments come on the heels of the DP World Tour making it so that those players who participate on LIV Golf 2.0 would not be able to take up membership on the European circuit. The league had previously granted conditional releases for those who called LIV Golf home. The decision was made ahead of a Ryder Cup year, giving the move added importance, as a player must be a member of the DP World Tour to be eligible for the European Ryder Cup team.
"You see Guy Kinnings coming out this week and saying that if LIV does go ahead with this 2.0 version, players that are thinking of going that direction, they are going to have to make a choice. It's either you play LIV 2.0 and you can't play the DP World Tour or you play the DP World Tour and you can't play LIV 2.0. I think this period of trying to double dip and do both is over."

title: David vs. Goliath MLB playoffs won't prove anything about a salary cap -- even if both sides will say they do - CBS Sports
description: The league championship series feature the top payroll in baseball along with three ranked in the 20s
body:
The league championship series feature the top payroll in baseball along with three ranked in the 20s
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    1:26 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        I'd rather not keep discussing this, but it's impossible to escape salary cap discourse in Major League Baseball in 2026.The League Championship Series round is upon us, which is the last four teams standing and vying for the piece of metal that is the World Series trophy. The two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers are in the mix, along with three franchises on the opposite end. The Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers are two of the five current MLB franchises with zero World Series titles in their history. The Cleveland Guardians technically have the longest drought, having not won a title since 1948 (when the Brewers and Rays didn't exist). In terms of history, it is Davids vs. Goliath, and that's where the payroll numbers stand as well.  Figures can vary based on loopholes and clever accounting (such as deferrals and back-loaded contracts). We'll use the competitive balance tax numbers from Major League Baseball. It seems like the number the league is taxing teams on is reasonable. Here are those payrolls, along with their ranking among the 30 MLB teams, for each of the final four in this season's playoffs. 
1. Dodgers, $432.8 million19. Brewers, $154.7 million27. Rays, $112.9 million29. Guardians, $93.1 millionWe could look at other places, as noted. The year-end 40-man roster salaries, for example, have the Dodgers second behind the Mets (monster deferrals drop the Dodgers way down to $339.6 million on their current 40-man) with the Brewers still 19th, the Rays 28th and the Guardians dead last in 30th with a payroll of less than $75 million.Regardless, we can see the gap here between the have and the have-nots -- or, more accurately, the big spender and the not-so-big spenders -- and that's one of the main focuses off the field during the league championship series this season, unfortunately. 
Before we go any further, and I'm gonna bold this so it doesn't escape anyone: No, this doesn't prove we don't need a salary cap. And, no, if the Dodgers still win the World Series, it doesn't prove we do need one.You can't just take results in small-sample playoff baseball, especially in one-year increments, to prove anything of the sort.I'm not immune to seeing the disparity in the payrolls and realizing it looks absolutely absurd. I just think it's a lot more nuanced than "spending more equals winning automatically" in baseball. 
Just look how close the Dodgers were to not winning in 2024 (they fell behind in the NLDS to the Padres) and 2025 (pick absolutely anything in Game 3 or Game 7 of the World Series). They might well win it all this time around, again, but they have an uphill battle to overcome an 0-2 deficit to a 103-win Brewers ballclub.The owner side in the upcoming CBA discussions would love nothing more than the Dodgers to win it all again so they can say the proof is in the pudding. I have no doubt that some on the MLBPA side would love to see the Brewers topple the Dodgers and point to the low-payroll teams competing in the Fall Classic. What if the Guardians win? We could look at the 40-man payrolls and say the team with the lowest payroll just won the World Series and WHAT'S UP NOW?!?!?
The MLBPA could easily argue that you can't act like low-payroll teams have no chance of competing with the likes of the Dodgers and Mets if, for example, the Rays and Brewers square off in the World Series after dispatching the Yankees and Dodgers, respectively? And conversely, we can't (or shouldn't) pretend that if the last four teams were, say, the Mets, Dodgers, Yankees and Blue Jays, the ownership side would suddenly become nuanced and say, "hey, this doesn't necessarily mean we need a salary cap." It would all be used as definitive proof.But it isn't. It's obviously more nuanced than that. One-year results don't necessarily prove anything at all. At the very least, though, the mix of these four specific teams in the LCS is pretty amusing heading into some inevitably contentious CBA talks.

title: Chicago Bears' Montez Sweat suspension: NFL suspends rusher for violating performance-enhancing substances policy - CBS Sports
description: Sweat will miss two important games before his return in November
body:
Sweat will miss two important games before his return in November
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:53 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Chicago Bears will be without edge rusher Montez Sweat for the next two games. The NFL suspended Sweat without pay for violating the league's performance-enhancing substances policy, the league announced on Tuesday. He will be eligible for reinstatement on Friday, Oct. 23.Sweat is set to miss Sunday's road game against the Atlanta Falcons and the Week 7 "Thursday Night Football" clash with the New England Patriots. His first game back from suspension is the Monday night trip to Seattle on Nov. 2, when the Bears face the reigning Super Bowl-champion Seahawks.Across the first five games of 2026, Sweat logged seven tackles and two sacks, the latter of which rank as the third-most on the team. It has been a relatively slow start for the pass rusher, whose 8.8% quarterback pressure rate is lower than any of his season-long marks from 2019-25. His time to sack of 7.18 seconds is also a career worst by nearly two full seconds.Despite the modest five-game stretch, Sweat remains vital to the Bears' defensive front, which is relatively thin on the edge. Just last season, he led the team in sacks, tackles for loss and quarterback hits, and he paced the squad in sacks for the two years prior. He earned the first and only Pro Bowl selection of his career in 2023 when he opened the year with the Washington Commanders and closed it in Chicago.Sweat's six turnovers caused by pressure in 2025 were a career best and ranked second in the NFL, per Next Gen Stats.
Bears' pass rush without Montez SweatSweat has missed only one game since his arrival in Chicago three years ago. The Bears logged three sacks in that 2024 loss to the Arizona Cardinals, but none of the players who recorded them remain on the roster. It will be primarily up to Dayo Odeyingbo and Austin Booker to step up during Sweat's suspension, and the former's status is in question after he left Sunday's loss to the Green Bay Packers with a quad injury. If Odeyingbo cannot play, James Lynch would be the next man up across from Booker.Booker is the team leader in sacks, quarterback hits and tackles for loss thus far, and he is responsible for a forced fumble, as well. He did all of that despite coming off the bench in each of the five games, so perhaps the pass rush will not regress as he steps into a starting role. Odeyingbo, meanwhile, also ranks ahead of Sweat with three sacks.The Chicago defense had a long day in Week 5 in its 31-7 rivalry loss, but excelled in Weeks 2-4, allowing a combined 28 points in three games. It may not have to shoulder as much of the load moving forward, as quarterback Caleb Williams is on track to potentially return from his hamstring strain on Sunday. The timing of Williams' return could not be more opportune, given Sweat's scheduled absence.
Here is how the Bears' schedule shapes up during and after Sweat's suspension:Week 6: at Falcons → Sweat suspendedWeek 7: vs. Patriots (Thursday) → Sweat suspendedWeek 8: at Seahawks (Monday) → Sweat eligible for reinstatementWeek 9: vs. BuccaneersWeek 10: BYE
